title: Greetings
description: Hello and goodbye across the day, with formality notes.

steps.title: A soft start
steps.body: Chinese greetings are relatively simple. 你好 is the universal starting point.

steps.title: Form vs. familiarity
steps.body: 您好 is more respectful than 你好. Time-specific greetings are also common.
bullets: 早上好 = good morning.
下午好 = good afternoon.
晚上好 = good evening.
再见 = goodbye.

steps.prompt: Match each Chinese greeting with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "Hello, how are you?":
steps.explanation: A warm, time-appropriate greeting — the foundation of any first impression.

steps.title: Listen · evening
steps.prompt: You hear this in the evening. What does it mean?

steps.partnerSays: 您好，很高兴认识你。你好吗？
steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: Nín hǎo, hěn gāoxìng rènshi nǐ. Nǐ hǎo ma?
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Hello, nice to meet you. How are you?
steps.prompt: Reply politely and return the question:
steps.explanation: "我很好，谢谢。您呢？" answers warmly and returns the question using the respectful 您. "再见" is a goodbye.

steps.title: Check · hello
steps.prompt: Which is the standard hello?
steps.explanation: 你好 is the universal hello.

steps.title: Check · polite
steps.prompt: Which is more respectful?
steps.explanation: 您好 is the polite form.

steps.title: Check · good night
steps.prompt: You’re heading to bed. You say…
steps.explanation: 晚安 is good night.

title: Please & thank you
description: Politeness formulas that open every exchange.

steps.title: Small words, big difference
steps.body: Chinese interactions expect 请 and 谢谢.

steps.title: Please & thanks
steps.body: 请 is “please.” 谢谢 is “thank you.”
bullets: 非常感谢 = thank you very much.
不客气 = you’re welcome.
对不起 / 抱歉 = sorry.
请 is also used before verbs to soften requests.

steps.prompt: Match each Chinese polite phrase with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "A coffee, please.":
steps.explanation: Combining a request with "please" — the cornerstone of polite interaction.

steps.title: Listen · reply
steps.prompt: Someone says 谢谢. A common reply is…

steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: Nín de kāfēi hǎo le. Sān kuài qián.
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Your coffee is ready. Three yuan.
steps.prompt: Thank him as you pay:
steps.explanation: "谢谢" is the natural thank-you. "不客气" (you're welcome) is what the clerk would say back.

steps.title: Check · shop
steps.prompt: How do you say “please” in a request?
steps.explanation: 请 softens requests.

steps.title: Check · reply
steps.prompt: Someone says 谢谢. A common reply is…
steps.explanation: 不客气 means “you’re welcome.”

title: Numbers 1–10
description: Count clearly for prices, times, and quantities.

steps.title: Count slowly
steps.body: Chinese numbers are regular and logical. Master 1–10 first.

steps.title: Notes
steps.body: Measure words (classifiers) are required when counting nouns.
bullets: 一本书 = one book
两杯咖啡 = two cups of coffee
Learn numbers with common measure words.

steps.prompt: Match each Chinese number with its numeral:
Arrange the stones to say: "Two coffees, please.":
steps.explanation: Numbers in context — the essential combination for real-world transactions.

steps.title: Listen · age

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: How many tickets do you want?
steps.prompt: Ask for two tickets:
steps.explanation: "两张" uses 两 (not 二) before the measure word 张 for tickets. "十五块" is the price the clerk would quote.

steps.title: Check · seven
steps.prompt: What is “seven” in Chinese?
steps.explanation: 七 is seven.

steps.title: Check · phrase
steps.prompt: “两杯咖啡” means…
steps.explanation: 两 = two (when counting).

steps.title: Check · age
steps.prompt: How do Chinese speakers say “I am twenty years old”?
steps.explanation: Age uses 岁: 我二十岁。

title: Introduce yourself
description: Name, origin, and a simple nice-to-meet-you.

steps.title: First contact
steps.body: A short self-introduction is enough: name, origin, and a polite close.

steps.title: 很高兴认识你
steps.body: This is the standard “nice to meet you.”

steps.prompt: Match each Chinese introduction phrase with its English meaning:

steps.title: Check · origin
steps.prompt: Best line for “I come from Belgium”?

title: Colors & simple descriptions
description: Name colors and describe everyday objects.

steps.title: Painting with words
steps.body: Colors in Chinese are straightforward nouns or adjectives.

steps.title: Color forms
steps.body: Colors usually come before the noun, often with 的.
bullets: 红色的车 = red car
蓝色的天空 = blue sky

steps.prompt: Match each Chinese color with its English name:
Arrange the stones to say: "a blue dress":
steps.explanation: Color + polite form — everything needed to express a preference in any shop.

steps.prompt: How do you say “red”?

steps.prompt: What is “black” in Chinese?
steps.explanation: 黑色 = black.

title: At the café
description: Order drinks and ask for the bill with confidence.

steps.title: A quiet table
steps.body: A handful of drink words plus a polite request phrase is enough to order confidently anywhere.

steps.title: Café culture
steps.body: Ask for the bill — servers rarely bring it unsolicited. Tipping customs vary by country.
bullets: For here or to go? — learn both forms.
A jug of tap water is often free — always worth asking.

steps.title: Check · to go

steps.explanation: 打包带走 = pack up and take away = to go.

title: At the market
description: Fruit, quantities, and polite requests at a stall.

steps.title: Market pace
steps.body: Markets reward clear numbers and a polite request. Pointing plus a word works — language makes it smoother.

steps.prompt: Match each Chinese word with its English meaning:

steps.prompt: How do you ask "How much is it?"

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: What would you like?
steps.prompt: Ask for three apples and the price:
steps.explanation: "三个苹果。多少钱？" adds to your order and asks the price.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: How do you ask the price in Chinese?
steps.explanation: 多少钱？= How much money? = How much is it? A core shopping phrase.

steps.title: Check · order
steps.prompt: Best for "three apples"?
steps.explanation: 三个苹果 = three apples, using the measure word 个.

title: Small talk & weather
description: Light conversation beyond hello.

steps.title: Beyond hello

steps.prompt: Match each Chinese word with its English meaning:

steps.title: Check · weekend

Stating allergies early is always wise.

steps.prompt: Order the fish:

title: Talking about plans
description: Express what you're going to do.

steps.title: The near future
steps.body: Each language has a simple structure to talk about upcoming plans.

steps.title: Patterns compared
steps.body: Learn the future/plan marker for your language.
bullets: Haitian Creole: pral + verb (no conjugation)
Korean: ~(으)ㄹ 거예요
Chinese: 打算 + verb or 要 + verb

phrases.source: What do you plan to do this weekend?
phrases.target: 这个周末你打算做什么？

phrases.source: I'm going to visit my parents.
We're going to watch a film.
She's going to travel to Shanghai.

steps.prompt: Match each Chinese word with its English meaning:

pairs.native: I want to / I'm going to…

steps.prompt: Arrange the stones to say: "I plan to visit my parents.":
steps.targetTranslation: I plan to visit my parents.
steps.explanation: Future marker + plan — two building blocks for any upcoming arrangement.

steps.title: Listen · structure
steps.prompt: Which uses 打算 correctly?

steps.partnerSays: 这个周末你打算做什么？
steps.partnerSaysTranslation: What do you plan to do this weekend?
steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: Zhège zhōumò nǐ dǎsuàn zuò shénme?
steps.prompt: Say you're going to visit your parents:

steps.title: Check · structure
steps.prompt: Which correctly uses 打算 + verb?
steps.explanation: 打算 + verb = plan to: 我打算吃 = I plan to eat.

steps.title: Check · translate
steps.prompt: How do you say "We will travel" in Chinese?
steps.explanation: 我们要去旅行 = We're going to travel.

steps.title: Check · delay

bullets: Haitian Creole: mwen gen yon doulè nan… (I have pain in…)
Korean: …이/가 아파요 (… hurts)
Chinese: …疼 / 我…疼 (… hurts)

steps.title: What time is it?

bullets: Haitian Creole: è (o'clock), e mwatye (half past), e ka (quarter past)
Korean: 시 (hour), 분 (minute), 반 (half)

steps.title: Calendar basics
steps.body: Learning days and months opens up conversations about plans, birthdays, and appointments.

steps.prompt: Match each Chinese word with its English meaning:

title: Talking about family
description: Name family members and describe relationships.

steps.title: Who's who
steps.body: Family vocabulary combines with "to have" and possessives for quick descriptions.

steps.title: Age-relative terms
steps.body: Korean and Chinese use different words depending on whether a sibling is older or younger.
bullets: Korean: 오빠/형 (older brother from woman/man's perspective), 언니/누나 (older sister), 남동생/여동생 (younger siblings)
Chinese: 哥哥/弟弟 (older/younger brother), 姐姐/妹妹 (older/younger sister)
Haitian Creole: frè (brother), sè (sister) — no age distinction

title: Grammar: articles & markers
description: How these languages mark nouns and structure sentences.

steps.title: Nouns and their markers
steps.body: Haitian Creole, Korean, and Chinese each handle definiteness and nouns very differently from European languages.

steps.title: Key differences
steps.body: No language in this group has gender like French or Spanish.
bullets: Haitian Creole: definite article la/a/an comes AFTER the noun; no gender
Korean: no articles; topic (은/는) and subject (이/가) markers do important grammar work
Chinese: no articles, no gender; measure words are required between numbers and nouns

steps.prompt: Match each Chinese word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "one book":
steps.explanation: A compact phrase that puts the article or gender rule into immediate practice.

steps.title: Listen · measure word
steps.prompt: Which measure word fits with "书" (book)?
steps.explanation: 本 (běn) is the measure word for books.

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: What is the measure word for "书" (book)?
steps.prompt: Answer correctly:
steps.explanation: Chinese has no articles or gender, but measure words (量词) are required. 本 is for books; 张 is for flat objects like paper.

steps.title: Check
steps.prompt: Which measure word fits with "书" (book)?
steps.explanation: 本 is the measure word for books: 一本书. 张 is for flat things, 杯 for cups, 件 for clothing.

steps.title: Check · gender
steps.prompt: Which statement about Chinese gender is correct?
steps.explanation: Chinese has no grammatical gender. There is no equivalent to le/la or der/die/das.

steps.title: Check · articles
steps.prompt: How does Chinese show definiteness?
steps.explanation: Chinese has no articles. Definiteness is shown through context, demonstratives (这/那), or word order.

title: To be & to have
description: The core verbs — and how they differ across languages.

steps.title: Workhorses
steps.body: The concepts of "to be" and "to have" exist in all three languages but work quite differently.

steps.explanation: Two core verbs in a single sentence — a powerful combination to internalize.

steps.title: Listen · identity
steps.prompt: How do you say "She is Chinese"?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: How are you?
steps.prompt: Say you're tired and hungry:
steps.explanation: Tiredness uses 累了 (got tired). Hunger uses 很饿 (very hungry). 是 is for identity; 有 is for possession.

steps.title: Check · 是
steps.prompt: How do you say "I am a student" in Chinese?
steps.explanation: 是 is used for identity/equation: 我是学生 = I am a student.

steps.title: Check · 有
steps.prompt: "我有预订" means…
steps.explanation: 有 = to have: 我有预订 = I have a reservation.

steps.title: Check · hungry
steps.prompt: How do you say "I am hungry" in Chinese?
steps.explanation: 我饿了 = I got hungry = I am hungry. 了 marks the change of state.

title: Verbs & patterns
description: How verbs work in these three languages.

steps.title: Verb patterns
steps.body: Haitian Creole verbs don't conjugate at all — the biggest advantage for learners! Korean and Chinese also avoid the complexity of European conjugation.

steps.title: Verb patterns compared
steps.body: These languages express tense and aspect very differently.
bullets: Haitian Creole: verbs never change. Aspect markers (ap, te, pral) are added.
Korean: verbs conjugate for politeness and tense, but not for person or gender.
Chinese: verbs never change. Tense is shown by time words and aspect particles (了, 过, 着).

steps.prompt: Match each Chinese word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I can speak a little Chinese.":
steps.targetTranslation: I can speak a little Chinese.
steps.explanation: The verb pattern in action — master this form and unlock a whole verb family.

steps.title: Listen · tense
steps.prompt: Which form shows a completed past action?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Can you speak Chinese?
steps.prompt: Say yes, you speak a little Chinese:
options: 是的，我会说一点了中文。
steps.explanation: Chinese verbs don't conjugate. 我会说 (I can speak) stays the same regardless of tense or subject.

steps.title: Check · no conjugation
steps.prompt: In Chinese, do verbs change based on the subject (I, you, he…)?
steps.explanation: Chinese verbs never conjugate. 说 = speak; 我说, 你说, 他说 all use the same form.

steps.title: Check · aspect
steps.prompt: What does 了 signal after a verb in Chinese?
steps.explanation: 了 marks completion or a change of state: 我吃了 = I have eaten / I ate.

title: Adjectives & descriptions
description: How descriptive words work in these languages.

steps.title: Describing things
steps.body: None of these three languages has the gender agreement of European Romance languages, which simplifies adjective use significantly.

steps.title: Key rules
steps.body: Adjectives work simply in these languages.
bullets: Haitian Creole: adjectives never change for gender or number
Korean: adjectives conjugate like verbs (for tense/politeness) but not for gender/number of the noun
Chinese: adjectives don't change form; predicative adjectives usually take 很 (hěn)

steps.prompt: Match each Chinese word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "She is also tall.":
steps.explanation: Agreement at work: the adjective shifts to match the noun it describes.

steps.title: Listen · adjective
steps.prompt: Which correctly says "He is tall" in Chinese?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: My brother is very tall. What about your sister?
steps.partnerSaysPhonetic: Wǒ gēge hěn gāo. Nǐ jiějie ne?
steps.prompt: Describe your sister the same way:
steps.explanation: Chinese adjectives don't change for gender or number. 高 (tall) works for everyone. 很 is typically used before adjectives in predicates.

steps.title: Check · 很
steps.prompt: Why is 很 used before adjectives in predicates?
options: It means "very" and is required grammatically
steps.explanation: 很 (hěn = very) is typically required before adjectives in predicative position: 他很高. Without 很, it implies contrast.

steps.title: Check · no agreement
steps.prompt: In Chinese, how does "tall" (高) change for a woman?
steps.explanation: Chinese adjectives never change for gender or number. 高 works for everyone and everything.

title: Saying no
description: Turn any sentence negative with simple patterns.

steps.title: Negation patterns
steps.body: Each language has a characteristic way to negate a verb. Learn the pattern, apply it everywhere.

steps.title: Patterns compared
steps.body: Negation is relatively straightforward in all three languages.
bullets: Haitian Creole: pa before the verb
Korean: 안 before verb/adjective, or -지 않다 after the stem
Chinese: 不 (bù) for general negation, 没 (méi) for past/existence

items.meaning: 没有什么 / 什么都没有

steps.prompt: Match each Chinese word with its English meaning:
Arrange the stones to say: "I don't like coffee.":
steps.explanation: The negation pattern in its simplest form — learn it once, use it everywhere.

steps.title: Listen · 不
steps.prompt: Which correctly negates "I like coffee"?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Do you like coffee?
steps.prompt: Say no, you don't like coffee:
steps.explanation: 不 negates adjectives and general actions (不喜欢). 没 negates existence and completed actions (没有).

steps.title: Check · 不 vs. 没
steps.prompt: Which is used to negate a completed past action?
steps.explanation: 没 negates completed actions: 我没吃饭 (I didn't eat). 不 negates habits/states: 我不吃肉 (I don't eat meat).

steps.title: Check · placement
steps.prompt: Where does 不 go in a Chinese sentence?
steps.explanation: 不 goes directly before the verb or adjective: 不喜欢, 不去, 不大.

title: Asking questions
description: Question words and patterns.

steps.title: Asking around
steps.body: Each language has its own set of question words and question-formation patterns.

steps.title: Patterns compared
steps.body: Yes/no and information questions each have their own structure.
bullets: Haitian Creole: eske at the start for yes/no; question word replaces the unknown element
Korean: question words in place of what they ask; -요? at the end for polite questions
Chinese: question words in place of what they ask; 吗 (ma) at the end for yes/no questions

steps.prompt: Match each Chinese word with its English meaning:

steps.explanation: A well-formed question using the key structure — polite, clear, and natural.

steps.title: Listen · why
steps.prompt: How do you say "why" in Chinese?

steps.partnerSaysTranslation: Do you have any questions?
steps.prompt: Ask where she lives:
steps.explanation: Chinese question words stay in the position of what they're asking about: 你住在哪里？(you live at where?)

steps.title: Check · word meaning
steps.prompt: How do you say "why" in Chinese?
steps.explanation: 为什么 = why; it pairs with 因为 (because) in the answer.

steps.title: Check · yes/no question
steps.prompt: Which word forms yes/no questions in Chinese?
steps.explanation: 吗 (ma) at the end of a statement turns it into a yes/no question: 你好吗？(Are you well?)
